compliance_deadlines: Within 5 days (without delay): Mandatory data-subject notification and breach reporting to PIPC/KISA upon personal data leaks affecting 1,000 or more individuals (PIPA Articles 34, 39-4, 48-4)
Within 5 business days: Target response timeframe for PIPC's Innovation Support One-Stop Service (regulatory sandbox, prior adequacy review, privacy safe zone, active statutory interpretation)
policy_extraction.penalties_summary: Adherence to the risk management model is voluntary and the self-assessment checklist cannot be used as grounds to establish a legal violation or to impose or aggravate administrative sanctions. Instead, the model serves as a safe-harbor incentive: best-effort adherence may be recognized as PIPA compliance or considered as a mitigating factor during administrative sanctions, and non-mandatory private entities voluntarily conducting a Privacy Impact Assessment under PIPA Article 33 are eligible for up to a 30% additional reduction in first-adjusted PIPA administrative surcharges.
policy_extraction.implementation_notes: Published 2024-12-19 by PIPC (developed with the Public-Private AI Privacy Policy Council), replacing PIPC's 2021 AI Privacy Self-Checklist and incorporating 2023 PIPA amendments. Establishes a 4-stage lifecycle AI privacy risk management framework (use-case classification, risk mapping, quantitative/qualitative measurement, organizational/technical mitigation) aligned with NIST AI RMF 1.0 and ISO/IEC 42001:2023, paired with CPO-led 3-Lines-of-Defense governance, value-chain role allocation across open-source and closed/API models, a 17-item self-assessment checklist (Appendix 1), and an empirical Korean LLM PET evaluation study (Appendix 2) demonstrating effectiveness and performance trade-offs across deduplication, input/output filtering, differential privacy perturbation, pruning, and machine unlearning.

risk_framing.rationale_summary: The model is dominantly framed around fundamental_rights, diagnosing AI's distinctive threats to informational self-determination, personality rights, and constitutional rights—including unlawful mass data collection, memorization and leakage of personal data, non-consensual deepfake abuse of biometric features, automated-decision opacity and discrimination, and mass surveillance/profiling. Fundamental_rights edges out innovation_enablement because protecting data-subject rights and PIPA legal principles anchors the risk taxonomy, mitigation catalog, and 17-item compliance checklist throughout the document. Innovation_enablement is a very close secondary frame: PIPC explicitly argues for a context-specific, proportional, risk-based, principle-based approach rather than preemptive uniform mandates so as to maximize AI's benefits, support sustainable AI development, provide safe-harbor regulatory incentives, and accommodate privacy-performance trade-offs empirically confirmed in Korean LLMs. Consumer_public_safety (deepfake sexual crimes, deceptive fraud/impersonation, cybersecurity attacks) and economic_competitiveness (AI as core digital-era competitiveness and synthetic data's economic value) appear as minor supporting rationales.

evidence_spans.quote_en: Generating non-consensual sexual deepfake imagery requires using victims' facial and bodily biometric data against their will, violating sexual self-determination, personality rights, and informational self-determination; deceptive misuse against victims, consumers, investors, and voters also damages reputation and rights.

This model was prepared to systematize AI privacy risk factors and present risk management directions and principles so that AI—a core competitiveness driver of the digital era—can be utilized in a privacy-friendly manner.
